taxonomy.subtopic: Usual interstitial pneumonia pattern and profibrotic signaling

questions.stem_html: A 71-year-old man has 18 months of progressive exertional dyspnea and a dry cough. He has bibasilar inspiratory crackles and digital clubbing. Pulmonary function testing shows reduced total lung capacity and reduced diffusing capacity. The accompanying paired diagram shows basilar subpleural reticulation with honeycomb cysts on high-resolution CT and patchy subpleural fibrosis with fibroblastic foci on biopsy. Which mediator most directly promotes the fibroblast activation and extracellular-matrix deposition that drive this disease?

options.text_html: Transforming growth factor beta
Interferon gamma
Interleukin 5
Bradykinin
Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor

questions.explanation_html: The imaging and histology show the usual interstitial pneumonia pattern typical of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Repetitive alveolar epithelial injury activates profibrotic signaling, especially transforming growth factor beta, which promotes fibroblast recruitment, myofibroblast differentiation, and collagen-rich extracellular-matrix deposition. The resulting temporal and spatial heterogeneity produces fibroblastic foci adjacent to dense subpleural fibrosis and honeycombing.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Interferon gamma is generally antifibrotic and macrophage activating; it is not the principal driver of myofibroblast differentiation in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Interleukin 5 promotes eosinophil growth and survival and is most relevant to eosinophilic airway disease.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Bradykinin increases vascular permeability and can contribute to cough or angioedema but does not explain the UIP fibrotic pattern.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor stimulates neutrophil production and is not the dominant profibrotic signal in this disorder.

questions.educational_objective: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis shows a UIP pattern with basal subpleural honeycombing, patchy temporal heterogeneity, and fibroblastic foci; TGF-beta is a central mediator of fibroblast-to-myofibroblast activation and matrix deposition.

media.alt_text: Original paired schematic of lower-lobe subpleural honeycombing, patchy fibrosis, fibroblastic foci, and TGF-beta signaling.

taxonomy.subtopic: Proliferative phase, GLUT1 phenotype, and beta-adrenergic blockade

questions.stem_html: A 10-week-old infant has a bright-red, raised lesion on the upper eyelid that was barely visible at birth but has enlarged rapidly. Because the lesion is beginning to obstruct vision, oral propranolol is started. The accompanying diagram shows the lesion becoming paler and softer within days, followed by gradual involution. Which cellular effect best explains the therapeutic response?

options.text_html: Activation of endothelial beta-2 receptors with increased cyclic AMP
Beta-adrenergic blockade with reduced proangiogenic signaling and vasoconstriction
Irreversible inhibition of cyclooxygenase in lesional platelets
Stimulation of mast-cell histamine release and vascular permeability
Selective destruction of GLUT1-positive endothelial cells by complement

questions.explanation_html: Infantile hemangiomas are benign endothelial tumors that enter a rapid proliferative phase during infancy and then gradually involute. Propranolol blocks beta-adrenergic signaling, producing early vasoconstriction and longer-term reduction of proangiogenic pathways such as VEGF-related signaling, endothelial proliferation, and survival. The drug does not selectively kill GLUT1-positive cells; GLUT1 is a characteristic diagnostic marker of infantile hemangioma.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Beta-2 receptor activation increases cyclic AMP and favors vasodilation; propranolol blocks rather than stimulates this pathway.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Cyclooxygenase inhibition is not the mechanism of propranolol and platelet biology is not central to infantile hemangioma involution.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Histamine release would increase erythema and edema rather than cause rapid pallor and regression.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: GLUT1 expression helps distinguish infantile hemangioma from many vascular malformations, but propranolol does not act through complement-mediated elimination of GLUT1-positive cells.

questions.educational_objective: Propranolol treats problematic infantile hemangiomas through beta-adrenergic blockade, causing early vasoconstriction and reducing proangiogenic endothelial signaling and proliferation.

media.alt_text: Original diagram showing infantile hemangioma proliferation, beta-adrenergic blockade, early vasoconstriction, and later involution.

taxonomy.subtopic: E7-mediated RB inactivation and p16 overexpression

questions.stem_html: A 46-year-old man with minimal tobacco exposure presents with a painless lateral neck mass. Biopsy of a cystic cervical lymph node shows nonkeratinizing squamous cell carcinoma, and examination reveals a small tonsillar primary tumor. Tumor cells show diffuse block-like p16 staining. The accompanying pathway diagram depicts a viral oncoprotein binding a cell-cycle regulator. Which molecular event most directly accounts for the p16 overexpression?

options.text_html: Viral E6 activation of telomerase with stabilization of p53
Viral L1 integration into the cyclin D1 promoter
Viral E7 binding and functional loss of retinoblastoma protein
Viral E2 activation of the APC beta-catenin destruction complex
Viral E5 inhibition of JAK-STAT signaling

questions.explanation_html: High-risk HPV-positive oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinomas commonly overexpress p16 because the viral E7 oncoprotein binds and functionally inactivates RB. Loss of RB-mediated restraint on E2F disrupts the normal negative-feedback relationship between RB and p16, producing strong p16 expression. HPV E6 primarily promotes degradation of p53, whereas p16 overexpression is most directly linked to E7-mediated RB pathway disruption.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: E6 promotes p53 degradation rather than stabilization; this does not directly explain p16 overexpression.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: L1 encodes a capsid protein and is not the viral oncoprotein responsible for RB pathway disruption.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: The APC beta-catenin complex is central to colorectal tumorigenesis and is not the mechanism of HPV-related p16 block staining.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: E5 can modulate growth-factor signaling, but diffuse p16 overexpression in HPV-driven oropharyngeal cancer reflects E7-mediated RB inactivation.

questions.educational_objective: HPV E7 inactivates RB in HPV-driven oropharyngeal carcinoma, releasing E2F and producing compensatory p16 overexpression; p16 is therefore a useful surrogate marker in the appropriate anatomic setting.

media.alt_text: Original pathway showing HPV E7 binding RB, E2F release, and compensatory p16 overexpression in oropharyngeal carcinoma.

taxonomy.subtopic: Fetal bladder outlet obstruction and renal dysplasia

questions.stem_html: A male fetus is noted to have oligohydramnios, bilateral hydroureteronephrosis, and a markedly enlarged thick-walled bladder. The accompanying sagittal urinary-tract diagram shows dilation of the posterior urethra immediately below the bladder, creating a keyhole configuration. Which lesion is the most likely cause of these findings?

options.text_html: Failure of ureteric-bud branching in both kidneys
An ectopic ureter draining below the external sphincter
Congenital absence of the trigonal smooth muscle
Obstructing mucosal folds in the posterior urethra
A urachal fistula connecting the bladder to the umbilicus

questions.explanation_html: Posterior urethral valves are obstructing membranous folds in the posterior urethra and occur exclusively in males. Fetal bladder outlet obstruction raises intravesical pressure, causing bladder muscular hypertrophy, dilation of the posterior urethra, hydroureteronephrosis, vesicoureteral reflux, and renal dysplasia. Severe obstruction can reduce fetal urine output, producing oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Bilateral renal agenesis can cause oligohydramnios but would not produce an enlarged bladder or dilated posterior urethra.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: An ectopic ureter commonly causes continuous urinary leakage in a female child and does not create a keyhole bladder-outlet pattern.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Trigonal smooth-muscle absence is not the typical congenital lesion producing posterior urethral dilation and male fetal outlet obstruction.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: A patent urachus causes urine drainage from the umbilicus and does not explain bilateral upper-tract dilation from urethral obstruction.

questions.educational_objective: Posterior urethral valves are obstructing folds in the male posterior urethra that cause fetal bladder outlet obstruction, a thick-walled enlarged bladder, keyhole dilation, hydroureteronephrosis, and potentially renal dysplasia and oligohydramnios.

media.alt_text: Original sagittal urinary-tract schematic showing posterior urethral valve obstruction, keyhole dilation, bladder hypertrophy, and bilateral hydroureteronephrosis.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content: Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
Posterior Urethral Valves. StatPearls. Updated 2026.
Khondker A et al. Posterior urethral valves, pressure pop-offs, and kidney function: systematic review and meta-analysis. World J Urol. 2023;41:1803-1811.

taxonomy.subtopic: Hapten sensitization and delayed type IV effector response

questions.stem_html: A woman develops an intensely pruritic, vesicular rash beneath a nickel-containing watchband 48 hours after wearing it. She had a similar but milder eruption months earlier. The accompanying skin diagram shows a small chemical binding epidermal proteins, followed by dendritic-cell migration and T-cell recruitment on re-exposure. Which immune mechanism is responsible for the current eruption?

options.text_html: Preformed IgE cross-linking on mast cells
IgG binding to fixed basement-membrane antigens
Circulating immune-complex deposition in dermal vessels
Complement-mediated lysis of hapten-coated keratinocytes
Sensitized T-cell recognition of hapten-modified peptides with delayed cytokine and cytotoxic responses

questions.explanation_html: Nickel acts as a hapten that modifies host proteins. During sensitization, cutaneous antigen-presenting cells process these modified proteins and prime T cells in regional lymph nodes. On re-exposure, memory T cells produce cytokines and recruit inflammatory cells; cytotoxic T cells can also injure keratinocytes. The delayed onset over 24-72 hours identifies a type IV hypersensitivity reaction rather than an antibody-mediated process.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Immediate IgE-mediated hypersensitivity occurs within minutes and produces urticaria or anaphylaxis rather than a delayed eczematous eruption.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Antibody binding to fixed tissue antigens is a type II mechanism and is not the basis of nickel contact dermatitis.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Immune-complex deposition is a type III mechanism associated with vasculitic or serum-sickness patterns.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Complement is not the principal effector mechanism; the lesion is driven by antigen-specific T-cell responses to hapten-modified peptides.

questions.educational_objective: Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed type IV hypersensitivity reaction in which haptens modify host proteins, dendritic cells prime T cells, and memory T cells mediate inflammation on re-exposure.

media.alt_text: Original skin schematic showing hapten binding, dendritic-cell sensitization, and delayed T-cell effector inflammation after re-exposure.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content: Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
Saint-Mezard P et al. Allergic contact dermatitis. Eur J Dermatol. 2008;18:271-281.

taxonomy.subtopic: Breslow thickness and vertical invasion

questions.stem_html: An excisional biopsy of an asymmetric pigmented lesion shows malignant melanocytes extending from the epidermis into the reticular dermis. The accompanying histologic schematic includes a vertical measurement from the top of the granular layer to the deepest invasive melanoma cell. Which feature represented by this measurement is the strongest pathologic predictor of survival in localized primary melanoma?

options.text_html: Breslow tumor thickness
Presence of melanin pigment within macrophages
Diameter of the radial-growth component
Number of junctional melanocytic nests
Clark level after controlling for measured thickness

questions.explanation_html: Breslow thickness is the vertical depth of invasion measured from the top of the epidermal granular layer, or from the base of an ulcer if present, to the deepest malignant melanoma cell. Increasing thickness strongly correlates with metastatic risk and survival and is central to modern melanoma staging. Clark level describes anatomic skin layers invaded but adds less prognostic information once Breslow thickness is known.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Pigment-laden macrophages may accompany melanoma but do not provide the principal quantitative prognostic measure.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Radial diameter is less predictive than the depth of vertical invasion.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Junctional nesting helps characterize a melanocytic lesion but is not the strongest survival predictor.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Clark level has historical value, but Breslow thickness is the more powerful and reproducible prognostic variable.

questions.educational_objective: Breslow thickness measures melanoma depth from the granular layer to the deepest invasive cell and is a major determinant of staging, metastatic risk, and prognosis.

media.alt_text: Original histology schematic demonstrating Breslow thickness measurement from the granular layer to the deepest invasive melanoma cell.

taxonomy.subtopic: Generalized proximal-tubule solute wasting

questions.stem_html: A 39-year-old man receiving tenofovir develops fatigue and bone pain. Serum studies show hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, and a normal anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Urinalysis shows glucose despite a normal serum glucose concentration, and additional testing demonstrates aminoaciduria and increased urinary phosphate. The accompanying nephron diagram highlights one tubular segment. Dysfunction of which process best explains this combination?

options.text_html: Hydrogen secretion by alpha-intercalated cells in the collecting duct
Generalized sodium-coupled solute reabsorption in the proximal tubule
Sodium-potassium-chloride cotransport in the thick ascending limb
Water reabsorption through vasopressin-regulated aquaporins
Sodium-chloride cotransport in the distal convoluted tubule

questions.explanation_html: Fanconi syndrome is generalized proximal-tubule dysfunction. The proximal tubule normally reabsorbs filtered glucose, amino acids, phosphate, bicarbonate, urate, and low-molecular-weight proteins through multiple sodium-linked transport systems. A global proximal defect therefore causes normoglycemic glucosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, bicarbonate wasting with type 2 renal tubular acidosis, and often potassium loss.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Distal hydrogen-secretory failure causes type 1 renal tubular acidosis but does not produce glucosuria, aminoaciduria, and phosphaturia.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Thick ascending-limb dysfunction resembles loop-diuretic effects and does not cause generalized loss of glucose and amino acids.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Impaired aquaporin insertion causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus with dilute polyuria, not proximal solute wasting.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Distal sodium-chloride cotransporter dysfunction causes a Gitelman-like salt-wasting pattern rather than Fanconi syndrome.

questions.educational_objective: Fanconi syndrome reflects generalized proximal-tubule failure, causing urinary loss of glucose, amino acids, phosphate, bicarbonate, urate, and low-molecular-weight proteins.

media.alt_text: Original nephron schematic highlighting generalized proximal reabsorptive failure and loss of bicarbonate, glucose, amino acids, and phosphate.

taxonomy.subtopic: Metaphyseal malignant osteoid production

questions.stem_html: A 16-year-old boy has progressive pain and swelling above the knee. Radiography shows a destructive metaphyseal lesion of the distal femur with a sunburst periosteal pattern and elevation of the periosteum forming a Codman triangle. The accompanying histologic diagram shows pleomorphic tumor cells surrounding irregular eosinophilic extracellular material. Production of which substance by the malignant cells establishes the diagnosis?

options.text_html: Mature hyaline cartilage
Amyloid derived from immunoglobulin light chains
Osteoid matrix
Keratin pearls
Mucin within glandular lumina

questions.explanation_html: Osteosarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal tumor defined by production of osteoid or immature bone directly by malignant cells. It commonly arises in the metaphysis of long bones in adolescents, especially around the knee, and may produce aggressive periosteal reactions such as a sunburst pattern and Codman triangle. The extracellular eosinophilic material in the diagram represents malignant osteoid.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Malignant cartilage production defines chondrosarcoma, which typically occurs in older adults.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Light-chain amyloid may occur in plasma-cell neoplasms but is not diagnostic of osteosarcoma.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Keratin pearls indicate squamous differentiation rather than a primary malignant bone-forming tumor.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Mucin-producing glands characterize adenocarcinoma and do not establish osteosarcoma.

questions.educational_objective: Osteosarcoma is diagnosed when malignant mesenchymal cells directly produce osteoid; it usually affects the metaphysis of long bones in adolescents and often shows aggressive periosteal reactions.

media.alt_text: Original paired radiograph and histology schematic showing metaphyseal sunburst reaction, Codman triangle, and malignant osteoid.

taxonomy.subtopic: Reactive CD8 T-cell expansion against infected B cells

questions.stem_html: A 20-year-old college student has fever, severe pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly. A heterophile antibody test is positive. The accompanying peripheral-blood illustration shows large atypical lymphocytes with abundant basophilic cytoplasm scalloping around adjacent erythrocytes. These atypical cells are predominantly which population?

options.text_html: EBV-infected memory B cells expressing CD21
Polyclonal plasma cells secreting heterophile IgM
Natural killer cells lacking antigen-specific receptors
Activated cytotoxic CD8 T lymphocytes responding to infected B cells
Neoplastic CD4 T lymphocytes with clonal receptor rearrangement

questions.explanation_html: EBV infects B cells through CD21, but the characteristic atypical lymphocytes seen in infectious mononucleosis are reactive activated cytotoxic CD8 T cells directed against EBV-infected B cells. Their marked expansion produces lymphocytosis and the distinctive large, irregular morphology. The response is polyclonal rather than malignant.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: EBV infects B cells, but the large atypical cells in the peripheral smear are mainly reactive T cells, not the infected B-cell population.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Plasma cells produce antibodies but do not account for the classic atypical lymphocyte morphology.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Natural killer cells can expand during viral infection, but CD8 T cells are the dominant activated population in acute EBV mononucleosis.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: The lymphocytosis is reactive and polyclonal; a clonal CD4 neoplasm would not fit the self-limited mononucleosis syndrome.

questions.educational_objective: The atypical lymphocytes of EBV infectious mononucleosis are activated cytotoxic CD8 T cells responding to EBV-infected B cells.

media.alt_text: Original diagram showing EBV infection of CD21-positive B cells and expansion of atypical activated CD8 T lymphocytes.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content: Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 4, 2026.
Dunmire SK et al. Infectious mononucleosis. Curr Top Microbiol Immunol. 2015;390:211-240.

taxonomy.subtopic: HHV-8-associated spindle-cell angioproliferation

questions.stem_html: A 35-year-old man with untreated HIV infection has multiple violaceous plaques on the legs and hard palate. Biopsy shows spindle-cell proliferation, slit-like vascular spaces, extravasated erythrocytes, and hemosiderin. The accompanying pathway diagram shows latent viral proteins promoting survival and angiogenic signaling in the spindle cells. Which infectious agent is required for the development of this tumor?

options.text_html: Epstein-Barr virus
Human papillomavirus 16
Human T-cell leukemia virus 1
Merkel cell polyomavirus
Human herpesvirus 8

questions.explanation_html: Kaposi sarcoma is an HHV-8-associated angioproliferative neoplasm. The spindle cells have endothelial lineage and contain latent HHV-8. Viral genes and inflammatory cytokines promote survival, proliferation, and angiogenesis, producing violaceous lesions with irregular slit-like vascular spaces and extravasated erythrocytes. HIV-related immunosuppression permits aggressive disease but HIV itself is not the required oncogenic virus.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: EBV is associated with several B-cell lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not Kaposi sarcoma.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: High-risk HPV drives anogenital and oropharyngeal squamous carcinomas rather than spindle-cell vascular lesions.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Merkel cell polyomavirus is linked to Merkel cell carcinoma, a neuroendocrine skin cancer.

questions.educational_objective: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 infection of endothelial-lineage spindle cells and is promoted by immune dysregulation and angiogenic cytokine signaling.

media.alt_text: Original histology and pathway schematic showing HHV-8-positive spindle cells, slit-like vessels, erythrocyte extravasation, and angiogenic signaling.

taxonomy.subtopic: Articular-cartilage matrix degradation and subchondral remodeling

questions.stem_html: A 67-year-old woman has chronic knee pain that worsens with activity and improves with rest. Morning stiffness lasts 10 minutes. The accompanying joint diagram shows asymmetric joint-space narrowing, marginal osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, and focal cartilage fissuring. Which molecular change most directly contributes to loss of the articular cartilage matrix?

options.text_html: Increased matrix metalloproteinase and aggrecanase activity in chondrocytes
Autoantibodies against citrullinated proteins forming synovial immune complexes
Deposition of monosodium urate crystals that activate the NLRP3 inflammasome
Loss of dystrophin linking muscle cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix
Defective type I collagen cross-linking caused by vitamin C deficiency

questions.explanation_html: Osteoarthritis involves failure of the entire joint organ, including articular-cartilage degradation, subchondral bone remodeling, osteophyte formation, and variable low-grade synovitis. Mechanical and inflammatory signals shift chondrocytes toward a catabolic phenotype with increased matrix metalloproteinases and ADAMTS aggrecanases, causing loss of type II collagen and aggrecan from cartilage.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Anti-CCP antibodies are characteristic of rheumatoid arthritis, which causes inflammatory symmetric polyarthritis and marginal erosions.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Urate crystal activation of NLRP3 causes gouty arthritis with episodic acute inflammation rather than the chronic radiographic pattern shown.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Dystrophin deficiency causes muscular dystrophy, not articular-cartilage degeneration.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Vitamin C deficiency impairs collagen hydroxylation systemically but does not produce the characteristic osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis of osteoarthritis.

questions.educational_objective: Osteoarthritis reflects mechanically and biologically driven chondrocyte catabolism, with MMP and ADAMTS activity degrading type II collagen and aggrecan while subchondral sclerosis and osteophytes develop.

media.alt_text: Original joint cross-section showing cartilage fissuring, joint-space loss, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, and catabolic enzyme activity.

taxonomy.subtopic: UV-induced epidermal atypia and progression to squamous cell carcinoma

questions.stem_html: A 74-year-old farmer has a rough, erythematous, scaly papule on the sun-exposed dorsal hand. The accompanying skin section shows parakeratosis and atypical keratinocytes concentrated in the basal and lower epidermis, with no invasion through the basement membrane. This lesion is a precursor to which malignancy?

options.text_html: Basal cell carcinoma
Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma
Malignant melanoma
Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans
Merkel cell carcinoma

questions.explanation_html: Actinic keratosis is a UV-associated keratinocytic neoplasm confined to the epidermis and is part of a continuum that can progress to invasive cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. Histology shows disordered maturation and atypical keratinocytes, often beginning in the basal and lower epidermis, with overlying parakeratosis. Invasion through the basement membrane marks progression to invasive SCC.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Basal cell carcinoma arises from basal keratinocytes but is not the typical malignant progression of actinic keratosis.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Melanoma arises from melanocytes and is not preceded by dysplastic keratinocytes.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans is a dermal spindle-cell tumor unrelated to actinic keratosis.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Merkel cell carcinoma is a neuroendocrine skin cancer and is not the expected progression of this lesion.

questions.educational_objective: Actinic keratosis is a UV-induced intraepidermal keratinocytic neoplasm that can progress to invasive cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.

media.alt_text: Original skin schematic showing lower-epidermal keratinocyte atypia, parakeratosis, intact basement membrane, and possible progression to invasive SCC.

taxonomy.subtopic: Mite burrows and delayed hypersensitivity pruritus

questions.stem_html: A 28-year-old man and two household contacts develop severe nocturnal pruritus. Examination shows excoriated papules and thin serpiginous burrows in the interdigital spaces and on the wrists. The accompanying epidermal diagram shows a female mite, eggs, and fecal material within the stratum corneum. The intense pruritus in an immunocompetent host is primarily caused by which process?

options.text_html: Direct neurotoxin secretion by the mite
IgM-mediated complement activation in dermal vessels
Delayed hypersensitivity to mite antigens and fecal products
Invasion of cutaneous sensory ganglia by the parasite
Eosinophil-independent release of histamine from platelets

questions.explanation_html: Scabies is caused by Sarcoptes scabiei mites that burrow within the stratum corneum. The characteristic itching and inflammatory papules largely reflect a delayed hypersensitivity response to mite proteins, eggs, and fecal products rather than direct tissue destruction. Symptoms may be delayed during the first infestation but appear more rapidly after reinfestation because of immune memory.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: The mite does not produce a neurotoxin that directly causes the characteristic nocturnal pruritus.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Immune-complex vasculitis is not the primary mechanism of ordinary scabies.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Scabies mites remain in the superficial epidermis and do not invade sensory ganglia.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Platelet histamine release is not the principal mechanism; the eruption is driven by host hypersensitivity to mite products.

questions.educational_objective: Scabies causes burrows in the stratum corneum, and its pruritic eruption is largely a delayed hypersensitivity response to mites, eggs, and fecal antigens.

media.alt_text: Original epidermal schematic showing a scabies mite burrow with eggs and fecal pellets plus a delayed T-cell inflammatory response.

taxonomy.subtopic: Resorption of distal alveolar gas after airway occlusion

questions.stem_html: On the second postoperative day, a patient develops dyspnea and diminished breath sounds over the left lower lung. Chest radiography in the accompanying diagram shows left lower-lobe opacity, elevation of the left hemidiaphragm, and displacement of the mediastinum toward the opacity. Bronchoscopy removes a thick mucus plug. Which mechanism produced the radiographic abnormality?

options.text_html: Leakage of air into the pleural space with loss of negative intrapleural pressure
Filling of alveoli by protein-rich edema fluid from increased permeability
Compression of lung tissue by a large pleural effusion
Absorption of trapped alveolar gas distal to an obstructed bronchus
Diffuse loss of surfactant causing bilateral dependent collapse

questions.explanation_html: An obstructed bronchus prevents replenishment of gas in distal alveoli. The existing gas is absorbed into the pulmonary capillary blood, causing the affected lung segment to lose volume and collapse. Volume loss pulls the mediastinum, hilum, and diaphragm toward the affected side. Removal of the mucus plug restores ventilation if the lung remains recruitable.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: A pneumothorax usually produces a hyperlucent hemithorax and, if under tension, shifts the mediastinum away from the affected side.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Pulmonary edema causes air-space filling without the marked focal volume loss and ipsilateral shift shown.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: A large pleural effusion compresses lung tissue and typically shifts the mediastinum away from the fluid collection.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Surfactant deficiency causes diffuse or bilateral atelectasis, especially in neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, not a focal lobar collapse from a mucus plug.

questions.educational_objective: Obstructive or resorptive atelectasis occurs when distal gas is absorbed after airway occlusion, producing focal volume loss and mediastinal displacement toward the affected side.

media.alt_text: Original chest schematic showing a mucus plug, distal gas resorption, lobar volume loss, elevated diaphragm, and ipsilateral mediastinal shift.

Patel TP et al. Resorptive obstructive atelectasis. BMJ Case Rep. 2019.

taxonomy.subtopic: Fibroproliferation beyond wound margins and collagen accumulation

questions.stem_html: A 24-year-old woman develops a firm, pruritic, progressively enlarging scar after ear piercing. The scar extends well beyond the original puncture site. The accompanying diagram contrasts this lesion with a hypertrophic scar confined to the wound. Which extracellular-matrix pattern is most characteristic of this lesion?

options.text_html: Loss of collagen with replacement by elastic fibers
Deposition of amyloid derived from serum amyloid A
Selective degradation of type IV collagen at the basement membrane
Failure to replace type III collagen with type I collagen during remodeling
Excessive collagen accumulation, with type III prominent early and type I prominent later

questions.explanation_html: Keloids are fibroproliferative scars that extend beyond the original wound borders and tend to recur after excision. They contain excessive, disorganized collagen. Type III collagen is prominent early in wound healing, whereas type I collagen becomes prominent in more mature keloidal tissue. Hypertrophic scars remain confined to the original wound and may regress.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Keloids are characterized by excessive collagen deposition rather than loss of collagen.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Amyloid deposition is unrelated to the fibroproliferative scar shown.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Basement-membrane type IV collagen degradation is associated with invasion and tissue remodeling, not the defining matrix pattern of a keloid.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Maturation can include a shift toward type I collagen; the defining abnormality is excessive collagen accumulation and growth beyond the wound, not a complete failure of collagen-type transition.

questions.educational_objective: Keloids are excessive fibroproliferative scars that grow beyond wound margins and contain abundant collagen, with type III prominent early and type I prominent in mature lesions.

taxonomy.subtopic: C5-C6 Erb-Duchenne palsy

questions.stem_html: After shoulder dystocia during delivery, a newborn holds the right arm adducted and internally rotated with the elbow extended and forearm pronated. Grasp is preserved. The accompanying brachial-plexus diagram highlights the upper trunk. Injury to which nerve roots best explains this posture?

options.text_html: C5 and C6
C7 and C8
C8 and T1
T1 and T2
C4 and C5 only

questions.explanation_html: Erb-Duchenne palsy results from injury to the upper trunk of the brachial plexus, formed primarily by C5 and C6. Weakness of the deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, biceps, and brachialis causes loss of shoulder abduction and external rotation plus elbow flexion and forearm supination, producing the classic waiter’s-tip posture. Hand grasp is preserved because the lower trunk is intact.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: C7-C8 injury would not produce the classic isolated upper-trunk pattern with preserved hand function.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: C8-T1 injury causes lower-trunk Klumpke palsy with intrinsic hand weakness and possible Horner syndrome.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: T1-T2 does not form the upper trunk and would not explain loss of shoulder abduction and elbow flexion.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: C5 contributes, but the classic upper-trunk lesion involves both C5 and C6.

questions.educational_objective: Erb-Duchenne palsy is an upper-trunk C5-C6 lesion causing loss of shoulder abduction/external rotation and elbow flexion/supination with preserved hand grasp.

taxonomy.subtopic: SERPINA1 Z-protein polymerization, hepatocyte retention, and elastase injury

questions.stem_html: A 34-year-old nonsmoker has progressive dyspnea. CT shows lower-lobe-predominant panacinar emphysema. He had unexplained neonatal cholestasis, and liver biopsy now shows eosinophilic periodic acid-Schiff-positive, diastase-resistant globules within hepatocytes. The accompanying diagram links hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum to alveolar destruction. Which cellular event causes the liver disease?

options.text_html: Excess secretion of a normal protease inhibitor into bile canaliculi
Polymerization and retention of misfolded Z alpha-1 antitrypsin in hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum
Autoantibody-mediated destruction of hepatocyte mitochondria
Failure of lysosomal glycogen degradation within hepatocytes
Copper accumulation due to defective biliary ATPase transport

questions.explanation_html: The Z allele of SERPINA1 causes alpha-1 antitrypsin to misfold and polymerize within the hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum. Intracellular retention produces PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules and can cause hepatitis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. The low circulating inhibitor level leaves lung tissue vulnerable to neutrophil elastase, causing early lower-lobe-predominant panacinar emphysema.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: The mutant protein is poorly secreted and retained intracellularly rather than excessively secreted into bile.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Autoimmune mitochondrial injury is associated with primary biliary cholangitis and does not produce the characteristic PAS-positive globules.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Lysosomal glycogen accumulation causes glycogen-storage disease and would be diastase sensitive.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Defective ATP7B transport causes Wilson disease with copper accumulation, not alpha-1 antitrypsin globules.

questions.educational_objective: Alpha-1 antitrypsin Z protein polymerizes in hepatocyte ER, causing toxic gain-of-function liver disease, while low serum inhibitor levels permit neutrophil-elastase-mediated basal panacinar emphysema.

taxonomy.subtopic: Enteric hyperoxaluria and calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis

questions.stem_html: A 42-year-old man with Crohn disease underwent resection of 70 cm of terminal ileum. He now has chronic steatorrhea and recurrent radiopaque kidney stones composed of calcium oxalate. The accompanying intestinal diagram shows unabsorbed fatty acids binding luminal calcium. Which change most directly increases his urinary oxalate excretion?

options.text_html: Increased hepatic synthesis of oxalate from bilirubin
Reduced renal tubular secretion of citrate with no change in intestinal absorption
Less calcium available to bind oxalate, leaving soluble oxalate for colonic absorption
Increased pancreatic bicarbonate secretion that alkalinizes the colon
Loss of gastric acid causing precipitation of oxalate in the small intestine

questions.explanation_html: Ileal disease or resection causes bile-salt and fat malabsorption. Unabsorbed fatty acids bind luminal calcium, so less calcium remains available to form insoluble calcium oxalate in the gut. Free soluble oxalate is then absorbed, especially in the colon, and excreted in urine, increasing calcium oxalate stone risk. Diarrhea-related low urine volume and hypocitraturia can further increase risk.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Bilirubin metabolism is not the principal source of enteric hyperoxaluria in Crohn disease.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Hypocitraturia can contribute to stone formation, but the defining mechanism of enteric hyperoxaluria is increased intestinal oxalate absorption.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Pancreatic bicarbonate secretion does not explain the increased oxalate absorption after ileal resection.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Loss of gastric acid would not create the characteristic fat-calcium binding mechanism; more luminal calcium binding to oxalate would reduce, not increase, absorption.

questions.educational_objective: Fat malabsorption after ileal disease or resection causes fatty acids to bind calcium, leaving free oxalate available for colonic absorption and producing enteric hyperoxaluria with calcium oxalate stones.

taxonomy.subtopic: Optic-chiasm compression of crossing nasal retinal fibers

questions.stem_html: A 52-year-old woman has headaches and gradually worsening difficulty seeing objects on both sides while driving. Formal perimetry shows loss of the temporal visual fields in both eyes. MRI in the accompanying diagram shows a sellar mass extending superiorly. Compression of which fibers produces this visual-field pattern?

options.text_html: Uncrossed temporal retinal fibers in both optic nerves
Right optic tract fibers carrying the left visual hemifield
Left optic radiation fibers in the temporal lobe
Crossing nasal retinal fibers in the optic chiasm
Bilateral macular fibers at the occipital poles

questions.explanation_html: A pituitary macroadenoma can extend superiorly from the sella and compress the optic chiasm. Fibers from the nasal retina cross in the chiasm and carry information from the temporal visual fields. Compression therefore produces bitemporal field loss. Actual field defects may be mixed depending on the extent and asymmetry of compression, but the classic localization is the crossing nasal retinal fibers.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Temporal retinal fibers remain uncrossed and carry nasal visual-field information.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: A right optic-tract lesion produces a left homonymous hemianopia, not bilateral temporal-field loss.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: A left temporal optic-radiation lesion causes a right superior quadrantanopia.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Bilateral occipital macular injury would affect central vision rather than selectively remove temporal fields.

questions.educational_objective: Suprasellar pituitary masses classically compress crossing nasal retinal fibers in the optic chiasm, causing bitemporal visual-field loss.

taxonomy.subtopic: Enzymatic fat necrosis, saponification, and hypocalcemia

questions.stem_html: A 49-year-old man is admitted with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and markedly elevated serum lipase. Two days later, he develops periumbilical ecchymosis and a reduced serum calcium concentration. The accompanying histology diagram shows necrotic adipocytes with basophilic calcium deposits around the pancreas. Which process most directly caused the hypocalcemia?

options.text_html: Calcium loss through glucosuria caused by transient hyperglycemia
Parathyroid-hormone suppression by excess calcitriol
Chelation of calcium by circulating citrate from liver failure
Renal calcium wasting due to distal tubular injury
Binding of calcium to free fatty acids released during enzymatic fat necrosis

questions.explanation_html: Pancreatic lipase released into peripancreatic fat hydrolyzes triglycerides into free fatty acids. These fatty acids bind calcium to form insoluble soaps, a process called saponification. Extensive enzymatic fat necrosis can therefore lower serum calcium and produce chalky or basophilic calcium deposits in necrotic adipose tissue.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Transient hyperglycemia does not usually cause sufficient urinary calcium loss to explain the characteristic fat-necrosis deposits.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Excess calcitriol causes hypercalcemia rather than the hypocalcemia associated with severe pancreatitis.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Citrate chelation is most relevant after massive transfusion and is not the mechanism shown in peripancreatic fat.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Distal tubular injury is not the primary cause of the calcium decline in acute pancreatitis.

questions.educational_objective: Acute pancreatitis causes enzymatic fat necrosis; released free fatty acids bind calcium and form insoluble soaps, producing saponification and potentially hypocalcemia.
